newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Australia PM treads a fresh path to Indonesia.
newsitem.headline: Australia PM treads a fresh path to Indonesia.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard will have a hard act to follow when he makes his first official visit to Indonesia this week.

His predecessor Paul Keating had built up a close relationship with Indonesian President Suharto and Howard would have to forge his own accord with the veteran statesman, leading political analyst Juwono Sudarsono said on Sunday.
"I don't think (the relationship) will have the same quality as the one with Mr Keating but it won't necessarily be too distant or cold. It will be good and correct," Sudarsono told Reuters.

Keating, known for his sharp and vitriolic manner back home, was close to the quiet and enigmatic Javanese president, defering to the elder statesman in a manner that some commentators said looked more like a father-son relationship.

In an intimacy built up during five visits in his four years in office, Keating was able to use his personal links with Suharto to conclude a landmark bilateral defence agreement between the two countries in December 1995.

"Now that Keating has gone, it is better that the more institutional aspects have been projected forward and that it transcends personalities," Sudarsono, also vice-governor of the official National Resilience Institute (Lemhanas), said.

Howard's two-day visit starting on Monday is seen as boosting ties, despite the potentially thorny issues of the appointment of a new Australian ambassador to Jakarta and Australia's response to recent political unrest in Indonesia.
Australian Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer, in Jakarta last week for trade talks, said Howard's visit reflected the dynamic relationship between Australia and Indonesia.
"It's about further building the economic linkage relationship between Australia and Indonesia," Fischer told reporters.
"In the first six months of the government we have clearly demonstrated our commitment to Asia."
Australia on Friday announced it had reached final agreement on its maritime boundaries with Indonesia in a move hailed as a breakthrough by officials in Canberra.
Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said the agreement was the culmination of more than 25 years of negotiations.
Indonesia is Australia's 12th largest trading partner and one its fastest growing markets, with bilateral trade worth more than A$3.3 billion (US$2.6 billion) in 1994/95 (July-June).
Howard, on his second overseas trip since taking office, visits Japan after leaving Jakarta early on Wednesday. The two-nation visit had earlier been postponed after his wife fell ill.
But analysts say the visit's sensitive points could centre on a call by Indonesian opposition figurehead Megawati Sukarnoputri on Saturday for Canberra to back her democracy push.
"I hope that the Australian government and people will support democracy in Indonesia," Megawati told Australia's Seven Network television.
Australian Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer ignored calls from her Australian supporters to meet her during his visit to Jakarta in July.
Canberra has also yet to formally nominate a new ambassador to Jakarta after its last nominee was rejected for being perceived as too critical of Suharto.

The rejection followed Indonesia's withdrawal last year of its nomination of a retired general as ambassador to Canberra after an outcry in Australia over his comments on the massacre of civilians in East Timor in 1991.

"The relationship sometimes varies between self-congratulation on both sides and at the other extreme mutual bashing with regards to East Timor here and Aborigines in Australia," Sudarsono said. (A$1 = 79 U.S. cents)
